sentences.text: Albertosaurus was a bipedal predator characterized by a large head, jaws holding dozens of large teeth, and small two-fingered hands.
Adults of this subfamily possessed slender builds with smaller skulls and longer lower leg and foot bones compared to their tyrannosaurine relatives.
The largest adult specimens featured a massive skull approximately one meter long perched on a short, S-shaped neck.
These animals grew up to eight or nine meters in length and weighed between 1.7 and 3.0 metric tons.
While adults typically reached about nine meters, some older individuals may have attained a length of ten meters.
Albertosaurus is one of only two known theropods, along with Carnotaurus, to have preserved feature scales.
The maximum bite force exerted by the posterior teeth reached 3,413 newtons.
A ten-meter-long specimen from the Dry Island bonebed is 28 years old, representing the oldest and largest known Albertosaurus.
By the age of two, juvenile Albertosaurus were larger than any other regional predator besides adults and faster than most of their prey.
The type specimen, a partial skull, was collected on June 9, 1884, from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation near the Red Deer River in Alberta.
Henry Fairfield Osborn named the genus in 1905.
Barnum Brown discovered a large group of Albertosaurus remains on August 11, 1910, near the Red Deer River.

The discovery of 26 individuals at one site provides evidence that Albertosaurus exhibited gregarious behavior, holding the largest number of individuals found at a single location of any large Cretaceous theropod.
Experiments showed that teeth with ampullas were more than 25% stronger than those without, similar to engineering techniques used in aircraft.
In 2001, William Abler observed that the striations on Albertosaurus teeth were so fine they could functionally act as a crack in the tooth.
Based on an estimated adult weight of 1.3 tonnes, the rapid growth phase of Albertosaurus occurred at a rate of 122 kilograms per year.
Researchers suggest that the end of Albertosaurus's rapid growth phase indicates the onset of sexual maturity, though growth continued at a slower rate for the rest of their lives.
Most known Albertosaurus fossils represent individuals that were at least 14 years old when they died.
The Dry Island bonebed assemblage includes one very old adult, eight adults aged 17 to 23, seven sub-adults aged 12 to 16, and six juveniles aged 2 to 11.
Currie hypothesized that younger pack members might have driven prey toward larger, stronger, but slower adults.
In 2024, Coppock and Currie reported evidence of cannibalism in Albertosaurus, citing tooth traces on a pubis that likely belonged to another A. sarcophagus individual.
In 2009, researchers hypothesized that smooth-edged holes in Albertosaurus fossil jaws were caused by a bird-like parasite that may have impaired the dinosaur's ability to eat.
The holotype specimen ROM 807 possessed a hole measuring 2.5 by 3.5 cm deep in its iliac blade.

Williams et al. (2026) presented evidence of preserved micro- and nanoscale histological features, including Haversian canals and lacunocanalicular networks, in bones of Albertosaurus sarcophagus from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation in Alberta, Canada.
Albertosaurus belongs to the theropod family Tyrannosauridae and the subfamily Albertosaurinae.
The genus is classified within the parent group Albertosaurinae.
Albertosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically from the latest Campanian to the early Maastrichtian, with a possible earlier Campanian record.
The animal lived approximately 71 million years ago.
Most Albertosaurus sarcophagus fossils are found in the upper Horseshoe Canyon Formation in Alberta.
Scientists disagree on the classification of the genus, with some recognizing Gorgosaurus libratus as a distinct species separate from Albertosaurus.
Fossils reported from Montana, New Mexico, Wyoming, and Missouri are doubted to belong to A. sarcophagus and may not belong to the genus Albertosaurus at all.
It is debated whether the Dry Island bonebed represents pack behavior or if the animals were driven together by environmental factors like drought or flood.
